source_receipt.title: KARMA: Training-Free Knowledge-Atomic Harness Evolution for Industrial Advertising Agents

original_quotes.quote: We introduce KARMA ( K nowledge- A tomic, R egression-Gated M odular A daptation), a training-free framework that externalizes knowledge into six typed modules and restricts adaptation to schema-checked, journaled mutations. Rule modules preserve stable identifiers and provenance, allowing an edit to be inspected alongside the evidence that motivated it. The full knowledge context remains available during inference, while model weights, business tools, and executable code stay fixed. Each edit has an explicit target, and validation measures its effect on agent decisions.

The knowledge state is a directory of six modules, K = { K m } m ∈ ℳ K=\{K_{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}} , where ℳ \mathcal{M} is the set of module identifiers (Table 1 ); the framework supports controlled edits to all six. Role, domain, and output protocol are typed text modules. Experience and constraints are ordered rule lists, (6) K m = ⟨ ( ι i , σ i , w i ) ⟩ i = 1 n m , m ∈ { exp , con } , K_{m}=\big\langle(\iota_{i},\sigma_{i},w_{i})\big\rangle_{i=1}^{n_{m}},\qquad m\in\{\mathrm{exp},\mathrm{con}\}, where exp \mathrm{exp} and con \mathrm{con} abbreviate experience and constraints, n m n_{m} is the number of rules in module m m , ι i \iota_{i} is a stable rule identifier, σ i \sigma_{i} its source, and w i w_{i} its text. Action descriptions parameterize 𝒴 K \mathcal{Y}_{K} and the local finish tool in Equation 5 .

For Qwen3.8-Max, the verifier groups 50 failures into ten modes. The Evolver adopts two of six proposals and generalizes them into rules E17 – E19 , while consulting successes to avoid overbroad changes. Validation improves from 36.88 to 48.75 (+11.88), so the gate retains the patch. Final knowledge, including edits from cycles 1 and 2, improves hold-out performance from 33.13 to 43.44 (+10.31), with both corrected and degraded cases. A corrected rationale explicitly cites E17 / E18 , illustrating rule-level traceability.

For Kimi-K3, the verifier finds 56 failures, including 40 wrong action types. Rationales implicate rigid budget-consumption thresholds; the Evolver deletes E06 and E12 and rewrites E07 . Validation falls from 41.25 to 34.38 ( − - 6.88), triggering restoration. The rejected patch is never evaluated on H H , so its hold-out effect is unknown. Conversely, Kimi-K3’s accepted patch on 𝒜 \mathcal{A} improves validation but regresses on hold-out (Section 5.6 ).

items.title: MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery

source_receipt.title: MolRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery

original_quotes.quote: MolRSI develops these workflows through experience-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), starting from configurations assembled from the resource library or retrieved from solution memory. Its search policy determines which workflows to explore, how to allocate search effort and how to refine and execute candidates.At each iteration, selection rules draw on workflows and scores in solution memory, combining performance on the current and related tasks with an exploration bonus [ ? ] for less-visited alternatives. Refinement memory supplies previous modifications and their outcomes to guide changes to the selected workflow. The agent then executes and evaluates the revised candidate, using execution memory to allocate resources and resolve errors. Search returns the workflow with the best development score within the task’s computational budget.

Persistent memory carries the outcomes of these searches forward to guide later decisions. Each attempt updates the stored workflows, performance scores, modification outcomes and execution records. These updates change subsequent search decisions within the task and remain available for later tasks. Search experience can also lead to revised or additional skills. Searches on new tasks therefore use a policy informed by earlier outcomes and generate further experience that revises the policy applied to subsequent tasks, completing the RSI cycle (Methods and Sections S1.1 , S1.2 and S1.3 ).

We assess the contribution of this cross-task policy adaptation by comparing MolRSI with and without RSI. Both settings use experiences obtained during the current task to guide search, whereas only MolRSI with RSI also draws on experience from previous tasks. Zero-search transfer tests direct reuse of previously developed workflow configurations without new search. Model fitting on target training data and evaluation on target validation data are retained.

MolRSI uses an Explore Agent to build the resource library. The agent searches for scientific papers and their associated code repositories, tools, benchmarks and algorithms relevant to the task. It uses the task description and data characteristics to formulate queries about data representations, model architectures, training objectives and domain constraints. For each retrieved resource, the Explore Agent creates a reusable skill describing how to use it. Each skill specifies the resource’s purpose, software dependencies, input and output requirements and execution steps, with references to available code, documentation and usage examples. The agent checks each skill’s syntax, dependencies and interfaces during library construction. When a newly constructed skill is first used for a task, the agent runs a usage example in an isolated environment. If execution fails, it uses the error messages and repository information to revise the code, dependencies or environment settings, then reruns the example. Skills that pass execution validation are tagged as validated and retained for reuse. Skills that still fail after repair are removed, so that only validated skills are available for subsequent tasks. Full implementation details are given in Section S1.1 .

Execution validation and reuse. When a newly constructed skill is first used, MolRSI runs a usage example in an isolated environment. Execution errors guide repairs to the code, dependencies or environment settings. The example is rerun until it completes successfully or reaches the repair-attempt limit. Skills that pass are tagged as validated and retained in the resource library for reuse. Skills that remain unsuccessful are removed.

items.title: VEvo-Harness: Causally-Guarded Self-Evolving Harness for Agentic Image Generation

source_receipt.title: VEvo-Harness: Causally-Guarded Self-Evolving Harness for Agentic Image Generation

original_quotes.quote: (1) Visual traceback. Unlike coding harnesses ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ; OpenClaw, 2026 ) with line-level tracebacks, visual critics provide only coarse binary feedback ( e.g. , pass/fail), because visual failures are continuous and multi-scaled. We construct a hierarchical verification tree that dynamically expands failed judgments into fine-grained failure modes ( e.g. , attribute binding), yielding structured root-cause signals that anchor experience memory and causally verified skill updates. (2) Visual continual governance . To prevent harness hallucination, we introduce a visual continual evaluator that estimates each candidate patch’s causal effect via counterfactual dual-arm replay under pinned skill routing, and admits only patches with positive estimated effects, thereby keeping the skill library causally validated. (3) A lifecycle-managed harness state. We organize persistent memory into working, instance, and pattern tiers, distilling root-cause-anchored repair episodes into reusable failure patterns that are causally verified before promotion into routable skills. The lifecycle enables the harness to accumulate causally verified experience and self-evolve monotonically across tasks. (4) A heterogeneous sandbox policy. Rather than hard-wiring the harness to a single prompt-rewriting tool, we expand its action registry into a heterogeneous sandbox, and route failures with a cost-aware policy based on visual traceback and persistent harness state. Our approach contributes threefold:

Formulation of Agentic Visual Generation. Let 𝒳 \mathcal{X} and 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} denote the multimodal input conditions and generated image spaces. Agent-based visual generation expands standard single-step inference by introducing a foundational primitive space and orchestrating structured workflows. The generation process is formulated as y = M ⁡ ( x , v ref , ℋ ) y\!=\!M(x,v_{\text{ref}};\mathcal{H}) , where v ref ∈ 𝒴 v_{\text{ref}}\!\in\!\mathcal{Y} represents optional reference images, M M is a frozen generation model, and ℋ \mathcal{H} denotes the agent harness, formalized as a composite system ℋ = ( 𝒜 , ℳ , 𝒢 , π ) \mathcal{H}\!=\!(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\pi) . Here, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is the execution sandbox, 𝒢 \mathcal{G} is the governance mechanism, π \pi is the routing policy, and ℳ = ( ℰ , 𝒮 ) \mathcal{M}\!=\!(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{S}) denotes the lifecycle-managed state, comprising the episodic memory ℰ \mathcal{E} and the persistent skill library 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . To handle complex visual synthesis, the harness orchestrates a directed workflow w ∈ 𝒲 w\!\in\!\mathcal{W} over a primitive set 𝒪 \mathcal{O} . In VEvo-Harness, accumulated experience continually updates ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} , forming a self-evolving agent 𝒜 t = ( M , ℋ t , w ) \mathcal{A}_{t}\!=\!(M,\mathcal{H}_{t},w) that generates image y = 𝒜 t ​ ( x , v ref ) y\!=\!\mathcal{A}_{t}(x,v_{\text{ref}}) .

Framework Overview. As illustrated in Fig. 2 (a) and Algo.1, VEvo-Harness forms a bidirectional closed loop between a frozen generation model M M and an evolving harness ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} , which integrates external tools ( e.g. , web search, code execution) to drive iterative generation via targeted interventions. In the forward flow, a user prompt is first parsed into verifiable visual constraints. The routing policy π \pi then queries the lifecycle-managed harness state (Sec. 3.3 ) ℳ \mathcal{M} to retrieve failure-aware episodic traces from ℰ \mathcal{E} and applicable heuristics from 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , which guide workflow construction and prompt enhancement. In the backward flow, failures of generated images are localized by visual traceback (Sec. 3.2 ) and addressed via the heterogeneous sandbox policy (Sec. 3.5 ). The repaired trajectories are assessed by visual continual governance (Sec. 3.4 ), which promotes only causally validated gains into the persistent skill library and retains the others as episodic experience. With generate–verify–intervene–memorize loop, the harness continually evolves through recursive self-improvement.

Self-evolution via Governed Knowledge Accumulation. Figs. 4 (a) and (c) link skill-update quality to sustained gains, as VEvo-Harness lifts its rolling-average GenEval2 score from 63.2 to 86.5 by distilling recurring failures into reusable skills. Without visual continual governance (VCG), gains collapse after a mid-stream peak near 78 to about 71.5, ending roughly 15% below the full model, since unverified updates pollute the skill library. Fig. 4 (a) attributes this collapse to admission quality, where No Gate admits 33–40% harmful patches and Text-only Gate settles near 16%, whereas full VCG reaches about 2% by 100 episodes, rising to 10% and 8% without the denied buffer or success preservation. GEMS and the stateless variant finish near 70 and 64.5, confirming that cross-task reuse requires persistent state. Thus lifelong memory and causally-guarded governance are complementary, with persistent state enabling reuse and counterfactual replay filtering updates before propagation.

At the end of iteration t t , the harness state is H t = ( C t , N t ) H_{t}=(C_{t},N_{t}) , where C t C_{t} is the entire source code that runs the agent, including the system prompt, tool definitions and implementations, context handling, and execution control, and N t N_{t} denotes the evolution notes stored alongside the code (Section 3.5 ). H 0 H_{0} is the seed harness. The harness runs on a fixed execution interface 𝒦 \mathcal{K} , which calls the model, executes commands, and records the entire run. Given a task x x , one run of the agent is τ = 𝒜 𝒦 ​ ( M , H t , x ) , \tau=\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(M,H_{t},x), (1) where τ \tau contains the model replies, tool calls, command outputs, and final artifacts. The grader of benchmark k k returns ( r , v ) = V k ​ ( x , τ ) , (r,v)=V_{k}(x,\tau), (2) where r r is the task score and v v is the test log or grading explanation.

3.2 Solver, Proposer, and Seed Harness Following the two principles of Section 1.1 , minimizing human-designed priors and giving the model maximal freedom to modify the harness, the framework makes three design choices: the solver and the proposer are the same agent, the outer program adds no analysis step, and the seed harness is minimal. The solver receives benchmark tasks and solves them, and the proposer receives an update task I t I_{t} that asks it to improve the harness. Both roles are played by the same agent with the same M M and the same H t H_{t} , and each runs in a fresh session. The outer program only dispatches tasks and packages run records. There is no step that organizes trajectories or summarizes errors. The update task provides three kinds of material: the source code and evolution notes of the current harness; the complete run records of the previous batch, including trajectories, task scores, and grader outputs, with both successful and failed tasks provided as is, without summarization or selection; and, from the second iteration of each stage on, the run record of the previous update session. The update prompt is short (Appendix B gives the full text). It tells the proposer that the modified harness will be evaluated on unseen tasks and on entirely different benchmarks, so it should look for improvements that generalize; that it may add or delete files and introduce any component; and that the notes travel with the harness to the next round. It also states the input limit per request and the budget of new lines for the current iteration. Beyond this, the prompt does not prescribe which records to read first, how to identify problems, where to start, or which part to change. During evolution, the proposer cannot access the internet apart from a few sites such as package registries, so it can rely only on the model’s own knowledge and these run records to improve the harness. The seed H 0 H_{0} is a single 49-line Python file (Appendix A ) containing a system prompt of a few sentences, a bash tool, and a minimal loop: call the model, execute the tool calls in its reply and append the results to the history, and stop once the model replies without tool calls. The seed has no output truncation, command timeouts, context compaction, or error recovery. Whether these are needed, and how to implement them, is left to evolution. The framework also neither partitions the harness into components nor restricts the scope of edits: apart from the execution interface 𝒦 \mathcal{K} , any part of any file in the harness can be modified, and files can be created or deleted.

H_{t},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (5) If the update session fails, for example because its edit does not pass the check or the session runs out of time, the outer program starts a repair session and then runs the update again (Appendix B ).

3.4 Two Stages: Multi-Task Pretraining and Continual Training Stage 1: multi-task pretraining (Iterations 1–5). There are K = 5 K=5 benchmarks, each split in advance into a training set D k tr D_{k}^{\mathrm{tr}} and a disjoint held-out set D k ho D_{k}^{\mathrm{ho}} . Each iteration takes b = 12 b=12 previously unused tasks from each training set to form a batch of 60 tasks: B t = ⋃ k = 1 K B t , k , B t , k ⊂ D k tr , | B t , k | = b , B t , k ∩ B u , k = ∅ ​ ( t ≠ u ) . (6) Together, the five iterations use each of the 60 training tasks of every benchmark exactly once, and the held-out sets are never run during evolution. Appendix H compares evolution runs that differ in batch size, i.e., the number of run records the proposer reads in one iteration. Stage 2: continual training on a new domain (Iterations 6–7). Starting from Iteration 5, the training tasks switch to tasks B t new B_{t}^{\mathrm{new}} from a new domain, mixed with a small number of old tasks A t A_{t} : B t = B t new ∪ A t , t ∈ { 5 , 6 } . B_{t}=B_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}\cup A_{t},\qquad t\in\{5,6\}. (7) The two iterations use different new tasks. A t A_{t} is drawn from the training tasks solved in the first stage, spread evenly across the five benchmarks. We call these tasks success anchors. They are rerun with the current harness, and their results are given to the proposer together with the records of the new tasks. This mirrors the practice in continual learning of mixing in old data, and its purpose is to prevent catastrophic forgetting. While modifying the harness for the new domain, the proposer always sees these old tasks, so each new edit has to serve them as well and cannot trade existing abilities for the new domain.

original_quotes.quote: So freezing the model does not by itself place a system in the safe, saturating regime: under (M1) the reachable set can grow while W W is fixed, and the frozen model guarantees only the eventual ceiling of part (i). Neither (M1) nor (M2) is a theorem; both are explicit assumptions (Remark 16 ). The criterion also runs one way only. Escape needs a gain that stays above a fixed floor, so a scaffold that expands while its gains shrink still levels off: growth is necessary for escape but not sufficient. Appendix G.4 works one example, an agent that writes a test-isolation script and reuses it in later rounds, which unlocks patches it could not previously check, with the model untouched.

6 Discussion For oversight: what to monitor. Frontier safety frameworks already test models with strong scaffolding, so the gap is not in how capability is elicited but in when re-assessment happens: it is largely triggered by training-side events such as a finished post-training run or a jump in effective compute ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Google DeepMind, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2025 ) , and the frameworks themselves treat scaffold-driven gains as an open problem (Appendix G.4 ). Under (M1), a scaffold rewritten between assessments can grow what a system reaches with no training event to prompt a new look. The quantity to monitor is therefore whether the scaffold is expanding itself, not only whether the weights changed. A loop that only re-samples is bounded by construction; one that rewrites its own tools or task breakdown is not (Cor. 4 ). Self-expansion is also a reward-hacking risk, since a system allowed to rewrite its own tests can game them rather than improve (Appendix G.4 – G.5 ). For practitioners. Two lessons follow, with five in Appendix G.3 . Spend on the first attempt, not the revision loop : later rounds mostly leave the code unchanged (Appendix Fig. 6 ). Upgrade the model before adding orchestration : orchestration cannot exceed the best worker’s ceiling (Prop. 5 ), and model tier outweighed every other factor we varied (partial η 2 = 0.497 \eta^{2}{=}0.497 ). Why model strength matters in the lab but not in production. Part B’s tier contrast explains roughly half the variance; Part C’s finds no gap between tiers. We do not resolve this, but the two contrasts differ in ways that could each explain it. In production, developers choose the model rather than having it assigned at random, and Opus is often used for planning while Sonnet does the execution, so a capability gap can be offset by harder or different work going to the stronger model. Part C’s adjustments for task type, repository and developer remove the coarsest form of that selection, not selection within a task type. The outcomes differ too: Part B scores whether the tests pass on a fixed task, Part C a structural proxy on whatever work a session took on. And the models differ: Part B compares Sonnet with Haiku, Part C two upper tiers. Random model assignment on matched tasks, or a functional outcome in place of the proxy, would separate these explanations; this data does neither. The decisive experiment, proposed and not run. The confounds above, and Part C’s human baseline, all point to one design this paper does not execute. Hold the model fixed and climb a ladder of scaffolds: (S0) no tools; (S1) the agent can run tests; (S2) it can also search or retrieve code; (S3) it can write tools during a run and keep them for later rounds. Run every rung on a fixed set of tasks with every round executed, including after a first pass, so neither confound of § 5.1 applies. Record two curves per rung: the gain per round η ¯ t \bar{\eta}_{t} , and pass@ k k coverage , the share of tasks on which any of k k attempts passes the tests ( Brown et al., 2024 ) . Coverage is our proposed practical stand-in for the reachable set, which we otherwise cannot measure: comparing rungs at the same k k asks whether a rung reaches tasks the previous one could not, rather than the same tasks sooner. It is a lower bound under a finite budget and depends on the tests, so it approximates the set rather than measuring it. The hypothesis predicts that within each fixed rung (S0–S2) gains shrink and coverage plateaus; that rungs adding new reach raise the coverage plateau with the model unchanged, which is (M1); and that only (S3), whose reach can grow mid-run, can show a plateau that rises within a run. It is falsified if coverage is flat across rungs, so these scaffolds do not expand reach and a model-level audit misses nothing on them, or if every rung decays like the human baseline whatever its reach, so the ordinary economics of editing explain the data. Open problems. Each is falsifiable, and blocked by something we did not do rather than something we found. (1) Build the harness of § 3 , keeping every attempt, focusing on failing specifications, and enforcing m ⋆ < k / 2 m^{\star}{<}k/2 : does it improve at the rate boosting promises, or does a new gap appear only in practice? (2) Run the vote across model vendors : do workers from genuinely different families satisfy Prop. 6 ? The measurement is cheap and has not been made. If they fail it, voting orchestration has no viable regime on real code. (3) Keep revising after the first pass : one re-run that does not stop on success would give the unconditional per-round curve this data cannot. (4) Hold the model fixed and vary the scaffold , the design above, and the only one that separates a fixed reachable set from the ordinary economics of editing. 6.1 Limitations The four below could each overturn a claim we make, or are why we do not make one; seven more that bound scope without threatening a specific result are in Appendix G.6 . • The slowdown is not specific to AI, which is why the evidence is descriptive. Human programmers before AI tools show the same shape of decay (§ 5.2 ). The data therefore place current practice in the bounded regime, but a fixed reachable set is not needed to predict that shape, so they cannot attribute it to one. Only a fixed-model design such as the one in § 6 could. • The per-round measurements are conditional. Because the harness stops calling the model once a task passes, the later rounds that would give an unconditional per-round curve were never run (§ 5.1 ). What we report conditions on a task still being unsolved, so the population shrinks and gets harder with each round (Sonnet 113 → \to 49 of 275), and part of any decline is a change of sample rather than of behavior. That applies to both the improvement edge and the gain per round; a fixed set of tasks with every round executed would remove it (open problem 3). Reading the strong model’s zero-crossing intervals as proof that revision does keep paying would over-read them as much as the pooled series over-reads the opposite. Part C does not measure the edge at all, so Cor. 11 is conditional throughout. • Rounds may restart rather than revise (an unchecked assumption). The model treats each round as an edit of the previous draft, z t = R t ​ ( z t − 1 , a t ) z_{t}=R_{t}(z_{t-1},a_{t}) , but an agent can abandon its approach mid-task and start over. Thm. 2 ’s bound on the best score so far still holds for such a path; what fails is reading the shrinking gains as revision saturating, and reading patches as building on each other. Pass/fail scoring cannot tell a restart from a revision, and we did not check, for instance by comparing patches across rounds. Part B’s independent arm restarts by design, and the underpowered feedback null cannot separate it from the others. • Observational data, model choice, and version pooling. In Part C the model tier is not randomly assigned: Opus is often used for planning and Sonnet for execution, so the tier contrast is partly a task-type contrast. The survivor ratio measures structural convergence, not whether the code works. Finding 2’s checks adjust for task type, repository and developer but not model version, which is why it is re-run by version. That the null survives rules out version pooling as the explanation without making it a demonstrated zero, and reading it as evidence against a capability effect would over-read it. Finding 3’s human comparison is likewise a comparison across eras. Orchestrator-worker topologies are treated formally in Appendix C .

items.suggested_summary_en: Under assumptions including monotone improvement and a fixed ceiling, the theory gives a criterion for gains to approach zero. SWE-bench and production sessions show descriptive saturation, without establishing its cause; the decisive fixed-model, varied-scaffold experiment remains proposed.

Identifying an invalid decision hypothesis does not directly determine how the restoration policy should be corrected. We therefore introduce a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism (CPRM) that explicitly learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify restoration decisions.
Given a hypothesis h h associated with reference condition z z and a modified condition z ′ z^{\prime} , their difference is represented as Δ ​ z = Diff ⁡ ( z ′ , z ) \Delta z=\operatorname{Diff}(z^{\prime},z) .
To adapt existing restoration strategies to changing degradation conditions, we introduce a revision operator that predicts the required adjustments: Δ ​ p \displaystyle\Delta p = U ω k ​ ( h , Δ ​ z , ℰ h ) , \displaystyle=U_{\omega_{k}}(h,\Delta z,\mathcal{E}_{h}), (10) p ′ \displaystyle p^{\prime} = Edit ⁡ ( p a , Δ ​ p ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Edit}(p_{a},\Delta p), where ℰ h \mathcal{E}_{h} contains previously verified evidence associated with the hypothesis. The predicted revision is represented as Δ ​ p = ( Δ ​ T , Δ ​ o , Δ ​ α , Δ ​ M ) \Delta p=(\Delta T,\Delta o,\Delta\alpha,\Delta M) ,
where the four components correspond to adjustments in tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions, respectively.
This enables the agent to learn how an existing strategy should be modified when degradation conditions vary, allowing the agent to adapt existing decisions beyond experience retrieval. To construct revision supervision, candidate restoration plans are evaluated under the modified condition. The best plan within the evaluated candidate set is selected as: p ∗ = arg ⁡ max p ∈ 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ′ ) ⁡ Q ⁡ ( ℛ ⁡ ( y ′ , p ) , x ) , p^{*}=\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}(y^{\prime})}Q(\mathcal{R}(y^{\prime};p),x), (11) where 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ′ ) \mathcal{P}(y^{\prime}) contains feasible candidate plans. The target revision is obtained by comparing p ∗ p^{*} with the original plan p a p_{a} . Meanwhile, we introduce a revision gate g ω g_{\omega} to determine whether the original plan requires modification. Specifically, the gate employs a lightweight two-layer MLP followed by a sigmoid function. It takes the encoded decision hypothesis h h , degradation change Δ ​ z \Delta z , and aggregated evidence ℰ h \mathcal{E}_{h} as inputs, and outputs a revision probability g ω ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) g_{\omega}\in(0,1) . The revision target is defined as:

The revision mechanism is optimized through: ℒ rev = \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}= 𝔼 ⁡ [ ℒ BCE ​ ( g ω , r ∗ ) − λ p ​ r ∗ ​ log ⁡ P ω ​ ( Δ ​ p ∗ ∣ h , Δ ​ z , ℰ h ) ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(g_{\omega},r^{*})-\lambda_{p}r^{*}\log P_{\omega}(\Delta p^{*}\mid h,\Delta z,\mathcal{E}_{h})\Big] (13) + λ r ​ ℒ ret , \displaystyle+\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}}, where Δ ​ p ∗ \Delta p^{*} denotes the target plan adjustment and ℒ ret \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}} is a retention regularizer that discourages unnecessary changes to previously reliable decisions.
During inference, the revised restoration plan is determined by: p new = { Edit ⁡ ( p a , Δ ​ p ) , g ω > τ g , p a , otherwise , p_{\mathrm{new}}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{Edit}(p_{a},\Delta p),&g_{\omega}>\tau_{g},\\
p_{a},&\mathrm{otherwise},\end{cases} (14) where τ g \tau_{g} is the revision threshold. The current degradation state is estimated from the input image, while its reference condition is obtained from the selected hypothesis.
To prevent unreliable revisions from affecting previously acquired capabilities, candidate policy updates are evaluated on independent transfer and retention validation sets.
Let π k \pi_{k} and π ~ k + 1 \tilde{\pi}_{k+1} denote the current and candidate updated policies. Their performance changes are measured as: Δ ​ Q tr \displaystyle\Delta Q_{\mathrm{tr}} = Q ¯ tr ​ ( π ~ k + 1 ) − Q ¯ tr ​ ( π k ) , \displaystyle=\overline{Q}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\tilde{\pi}_{k+1})-\overline{Q}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\pi_{k}), (15) Δ ​ Q ret \displaystyle\Delta Q_{\mathrm{ret}} = Q ¯ ret ​ ( π ~ k + 1 ) − Q ¯ ret ​ ( π k ) , \displaystyle=\overline{Q}_{\mathrm{ret}}(\tilde{\pi}_{k+1})-\overline{Q}_{\mathrm{ret}}(\pi_{k}), where the transfer set evaluates decisions under changed degradation conditions, while the retention set measures performance on previously learned conditions.
The candidate update is accepted when 𝕀 [ Δ Q tr ≥ δ tr ∧ Δ Q ret ≥ − ϵ ret ] \mathbb{I}\left[\Delta Q_{\mathrm{tr}}\geq\delta_{\mathrm{tr}}\land\Delta Q_{\mathrm{ret}}\geq-\epsilon_{\mathrm{ret}}\right] , δ tr \delta_{\mathrm{tr}} denotes the required improvement and ϵ ret \epsilon_{\mathrm{ret}} specifies the allowable performance reduction.
Updates failing these criteria are rejected. Successful revisions update the agent policy and its revision mechanism, which subsequently guide new hypothesis discovery and task generation. Through this process, RecurIR progressively improves not only restoration decisions but also its ability to determine when and how those decisions should be revised.

items.title: ForgeSystem: An Architecture for Demand-Specific Artefact Production with AI Agents

source_receipt.title: ForgeSystem: An Architecture for Demand-Specific Artefact Production with AI Agents

original_quotes.quote: 3.3 Recursive self-improvement Forged-artefact feedback. Delivered forged artefacts and their components can serve as starting points for subsequent construction. The Forge Archive stores each delivered artefact together with its demand and construction trace, and the forge scheduler can select a starting point from it (Section 3.1 ). Depending on the differences between the selected artefact and the demand, subsequent construction can directly reuse, adapt or reconstruct it, or combine components from several artefacts. When the archive already holds a forged artefact that meets the demand, the forge scheduler still estimates the expected benefit and cost of forging again, with the benefit measured against this forged artefact; if the expected benefit exceeds the expected cost (Eq. ( 1 )), it forges again with this forged artefact as the starting point. Such reuse changes how exploration is organised: solved parts need not be rebuilt, new attempts can focus on the unmet parts of the demand, and existing components can be recombined. Harness self-improvement. We incorporate ontology engineering into the harness, organising domain concepts, component relations, dependencies and applicability conditions into a retrievable knowledge graph that provides agents with the domain knowledge needed for construction. Execution feedback guides changes to context provision, tool use, the organisation of exploration, and testing. After the harness is updated, the system compares artefact quality and production cost on subsequent forging tasks to assess whether these changes improve the production process. Self-improvement through training. Because archived delivered artefacts and their construction traces have already passed independent judgement, they provide quality-screened examples for supervised learning of implementation choices, cross-component design and search. Archived demands can also serve as reinforcement-learning tasks, with rewards assigned by the verification side to newly generated rollouts. Training requires long-term investment and validation to internalise experience. Updated models return to forging, closing an RSI loop in the narrow sense: judgement-screened construction traces train the model that produces subsequent artefacts, with gains assessed through subsequent artefact quality, construction cost and search efficiency.

9 Scope and bottlenecks The scope and bottlenecks of Forge centre on three factors. Specialisation benefits. Rebuilding offers limited value when general-purpose solutions already satisfy a demand or demand differences yield little performance or efficiency gain. Specialisation must also preserve necessary interoperability conventions. Complete production cost. Cheaper model calls do not imply proportionately cheaper delivery. Experimentation, verification, integration and human intervention may remain costly, particularly where reliable evaluation criteria are unavailable. Returns from accumulated experience. Prior work shows that construction experience can improve model performance Pan et al. (2025) ; Hubert et al. (2026) , but repetitive trajectories and limited learning signals may lead to diminishing returns. Sustained capability gains from the outer loop require validation over multiple rounds of construction and training.
